title: Namo
hookLine: a toast that never says the name, and a chant that does the same
tomorrow: the Blessed One, the Lord, the Fortunate One: which is it?

cards: Some wedding toasts never use the groom's name. Here's to him: the one who drove everyone to the airport at dawn, the one who still calls his grandmother on Sundays. Nobody in the room wonders who.
The first line of the Pali homage works the same way, and it's a small puzzle once you see it. Namo tassa: homage to him. Him who?
The line never says Siddhattha. It never says Gotama. Where a name should go, there's a word that only points.

teach.h: NAMO: A BOW IN A WORD.
teach.b: Start with namo. It means homage: a bow, put into a word. Short a, long o, by the rule of two days ago.

teach.h: NAMAS, NAM MÔ: ONE OLD WORD.
teach.b: Sanskrit has the same word as namas, the one tucked inside namaste.

And Vietnamese Buddhists, at home and in temple, say nam mô before a Buddha's name, as in nam mô A Di Đà Phật, homage to the Buddha Amitabha: the same old word, carried into Vietnamese by way of Chinese.
One bow, many mouths. Then tassa: to him, to that one.

teach.h: TASSA: A POINTER, NOT A NAME.
teach.b: A pointer, not a name. So the puzzle. Why point instead of name?

Three titles line up behind tassa: bhagavato, the Blessed One; arahato, the worthy one; samma-sambuddhassa, the one fully awake by himself. Each ends the way tassa ends, so each points back at the same him.
The chant never explains its choice.

But here's one way to hear it: the homage goes to what he became, not to his family name. You'll meet one title a day for three days. By the end of the week the whole line will be yours, word by word.
For now, just the first two: namo tassa. Homage to him.

how: In Theravada temples the homage, namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa, is chanted before the refuges and precepts; in Vietnamese temples and homes, people say nam mô before a Buddha's name.

o: the Buddha's own name, said first
a word for the temple's main hall
homage: a bow put into a word

games.q: the first two words — tap the pairs.
p: homage: a bow in a word

s: namo is a name of the Buddha
namo means homage. the line never names him; tassa points, and the titles follow.
namaste and namo share a word
Sanskrit namas, homage, is the word inside namaste; namo is its form in the chant.
the homage says Gotama somewhere in it
it never does. after tassa come three titles, each pointing back at him.

games.q: you're explaining the homage to a friend who asks, so who exactly is tassa? what's the best answer?
o: him: the word points, and the three titles after it say who he became.
the temple: tassa is the name of the place where the chant is said.
whoever is leading the chant that night, as a sign of respect.
games.why: tassa just means to him. the homage never gives his family name; bhagavato, arahato and samma-sambuddhassa line up behind it instead.

practice: Write namo tassa on a scrap of paper, slowly, in your best letters, the way you'd letter a card.
Then say it once, out loud, short a, long o, a small bow carried in two words, and let the paper sit in front of you while the breath settles.

wordCard.voice: Namo. Homage: a bow put into a word, the first sound of the Pali homage, and the same sound inside namaste and nam mô. Word four of a little Pali.

orig.note: namo tassa in Devanagari letters: homage to him, the opening words of the Pali homage.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: homage to him, a bow that points before it names. See you tomorrow.
